venues.a: Hof bei Salzburg / Lake Fuschl (≈25 min east of the Old Town)
venues.d: A 15th-century lakeside castle reborn by Rosewood in 2024 — the region's most complete luxury retreat, set in its own estate on Lake Fuschl.

venues.a: Neustadt / right bank, on the Salzach facing the Old Town
venues.d: Salzburg's grande dame — a riverside palace of the famed Sacher family, with the finest Old Town views in the city.

venues.a: Mönchsberg / the city mountain, above the Old Town
venues.d: A small castle-hotel in a private park atop the Mönchsberg — seclusion and forest quiet, minutes above the city by the mountain lift.

venues.n: Hotel Goldener Hirsch, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.a: Altstadt / Getreidegasse, the heart of the Old Town
venues.d: An inn since 1564 on Salzburg's grandest shopping street — beamed, antique-filled rooms with centuries of pedigree, now under Marriott's Luxury Collection.
A capable, spacious modern grand hotel right on the Mirabell Gardens — reliable comfort and easy access to both riverbanks.

venues.a: Hangar-7, by the airport (≈10 min from the Old Town)
venues.d: The world's only rotating-guest-chef fine-dining room — a different acclaimed chef every month, under culinary director Martin Klein, inside Red Bull's glass Hangar-7.

venues.a: Söllheim / a converted metal factory on the city's edge
venues.d: Andreas Senn's precise, contemporary cooking in a raw industrial hall — Salzburg's other two-star, and one of Austria's most exciting tables.
Fine dining reimagined as elegant, cone-served small plates — a singular concept on the Old Town's grandest street, from the Red Bull stable.

venues.a: Neustadt / at the foot of the Mönchsberg
venues.d: Andreas Kaiblinger's flavour-forward, contemporary Austrian cooking, with his wife Andrea's warm front-of-house and a considered wine list.
Simon Wagner's delicate, produce-led cooking in a glass pavilion high above the city — food and fortress views in one sitting.

venues.a: Hallwang / Söllheim (≈15 min north-east of the Old Town)
venues.d: Jürgen Vigne's bold, ingredient-driven cooking in a 17th-century parish house — one of the region's longest-running serious kitchens.

venues.a: Salzburg / Liefering, west of the centre
venues.d: A family-run country house of hearty, honest Austrian cooking — a beautiful garden, a serious cellar and terrific value.
The Obauer brothers' legendary two-star — a lifetime of refined alpine-Austrian cooking, worth the drive out toward the Werfen ice caves.

One of the largest and best-preserved medieval fortresses in Europe, begun in 1077 and never once taken by siege, crowning the city on its rock. A private guide can time the reserved funicular ride so grandparents skip the climb, and the ramparts give the family the definitive photograph of Salzburg spread below.

One of the world's oldest operating funiculars, running up to the fortress since 1892 on the line of an even older 16th-century hoist. The 54-second ride spares elders and small children the steep cobbled walk and is a small delight in itself.

A tight weave of Baroque squares, archways and merchant courtyards between the fortress and the river, walkable end to end and closed to most traffic. A private walking guide turns it from a pretty maze into a legible story of prince-archbishops, Mozart and money.

Salzburg's famous shopping lane, narrow and canyon-like, hung with wrought-iron guild signs that even global luxury houses must obey. The address of Mozart's birthplace at number 9 and a good spot to combine boutiques with a discreet, unhurried browse.

The yellow house where Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in 1756 and lived his first seventeen years, now a museum of his violins, letters and portraits. The essential Mozart pilgrimage, best taken with a private guide who can bring the child prodigy vividly to life for a multi-generational group.

The larger apartment across the river where the Mozart family moved in 1773, with the composer's own fortepiano and a quieter, more reflective feel than the crowded birthplace. The two houses together give the fuller portrait of the man behind the myth.

The vast early-Baroque cathedral where Mozart was baptised and later served as organist, its bronze doors, marble facade and 4,000-pipe organs setting the scale of the prince-archbishops' ambition. Cool, grand and free to enter for a moment of calm between sights.

A single connected circuit through the Residenz state rooms, the cathedral terrace and galleries, and St Peter's museum — the seat of church-and-state power reopened after two centuries closed. A rewarding, weather-proof morning with a private guide for a family that wants depth over crowds.

The prince-archbishops' city palace, a suite of gilded staterooms where the young Mozart performed for the court, hung with Rembrandt, Rubens and Titian in the adjoining gallery. Opulent and intimate — the private face of Salzburg's rulers.

Founded in 696, the oldest monastery in the German-speaking world, its abbey church a layered jewel of Romanesque bones dressed in Rococo. Still a working Benedictine community, quiet and deeply atmospheric.

One of Salzburg's oldest burial grounds, a wrought-iron garden of arcaded family vaults set against the sheer Mönchsberg cliff — where Mozart's sister Nannerl rests, and the visual model for The Sound of Music's escape scene. Serene, exquisite and endlessly photogenic.

Early Christian chapels and hermit cells hewn straight into the rock face above the cemetery, reached by a steep stair to little rooms with a startling view down over the graves. A short, memorable climb for those steady on their feet.

The oldest continuously operating convent in the German-speaking world, founded around 714, where the real Maria von Trapp was a novice before her marriage. A hushed, working nunnery just above the Old Town, and the true starting point of the Sound of Music story.

A quietly extraordinary church where a dark Romanesque nave opens into a soaring Gothic choir crowned by a golden Baroque high altar — three eras stacked in one space. Often overlooked between the bigger sights, and all the better for it.

venues.n: Mozart Dinner Concert at St Peter Stiftskulinarium
venues.d: A candlelit evening of Mozart arias and a period three-course dinner in the Baroque hall of Europe's oldest restaurant, in business since 803 and once graced by Mozart himself. A romantic, only-in-Salzburg night; the kitchen will handle vegetarian and Indian dietary needs with advance notice.

venues.a: Festival District, Altstadt (seasonal — late July to end August)
venues.d: Founded in 1920, the world's foremost festival of opera and drama, filling the Grosses Festspielhaus, the Felsenreitschule carved into the cliff, and the squares with the finest voices alive. The reason to plan a summer trip well in advance; the hardest ticket in classical music, and worth every effort to secure.

A theatre carved into the living rock of the Mönchsberg, its stone arcades once a riding school and now a spectacular festival stage — and the concert-hall backdrop of the final Sound of Music scene. Extraordinary even empty; unforgettable during a performance.

The world's centre of Mozart scholarship, with two elegant concert halls, the family's letters and instruments, and the small garden pavilion where he is said to have composed The Magic Flute. The serious counterpoint to the tourist Mozart, for those who want the real music.

A crisp modernist gallery of 20th- and 21st-century art set 60 metres above the Old Town, reached by a dedicated lift that rises in half a minute. The art is strong, but the terrace and its restaurant hold the finest full panorama of the city and Alps — a serene lunch with a view.

A green cliff-top promenade running the length of the Old Town, dotted with lookouts, the Richterhöhe bastion and quiet benches, easily reached by lift and level once you are up. The locals' escape from the crowds below, with the fortress on one side and the mountains on the other.

The wooded hill facing the fortress, climbed by a Stations-of-the-Cross path to a Capuchin monastery, deer, and some of the best views back at the Old Town skyline. Stefan Zweig once lived here; a peaceful, uncrowded hour for those who like to walk.

Wide, flat promenades along the fast green river linking the two halves of the city, lined with pastel facades and lace-locked footbridges, the fortress always in view. The easiest, loveliest stroll in Salzburg — perfect for a multi-generational group at any pace.

The city's flagship history museum in the New Residence palace, elegantly telling Salzburg's story from Roman roots through the prince-archbishops to the Festival. An award-winning, unhurried indoor option when the weather turns.

A prince-archbishop's 1615 pleasure villa surrounded by Mannerist water gardens engineered to soak unsuspecting guests — grottoes, a hydraulic mechanical theatre and hidden jets that delight children and grandparents alike. A joyous, easy half-day just outside town; take a private guide who knows which seats stay dry.

The glass garden pavilion of "Sixteen Going on Seventeen," moved to the Hellbrunn grounds and freely visitable in the park. A quick, sentimental stop that pairs naturally with the trick fountains for fans of the film.

A former quarry turned open-air stage, where in 1617 the first opera performed outside Italy was staged — arguably the oldest such theatre north of the Alps. A hidden, moss-softened amphitheatre a short walk from the palace, magical and almost always empty.

The half-day circuit of film settings — Leopoldskron's lake terrace, Frohnburg's gates, the Mirabell gardens, the Nonnberg convent and the Mondsee wedding church. Best done privately by car so the family sets its own pace and skips the sing-along coach.

A Rococo lakeside palace, once Max Reinhardt's and the lake-terrace "von Trapp villa" of The Sound of Music, now an exclusive private hotel and seminar house. Its mirrored Venetian Room and gardens can be experienced over afternoon tea or a stay — the film's most beautiful real address.

The visitor world of Austria's largest private brewery, brewing since 1492, with a museum, a garden and generous tastings of unfiltered beer. A relaxed, hands-on afternoon for the beer-curious and an easy change of register from all the Baroque.

venues.a: St. Leonhard, south of the city
venues.d: An eight-minute glass gondola from the city's doorstep to the top of the Untersberg at 1,776 metres, where a short walk delivers a sweeping Alpine panorama across Salzburg and Bavaria. The quickest way to put the family on a real mountain summit before lunch — take warm layers even in summer.

The rounded local mountain reached by a scenic road to a summit of paragliders, walking trails and a 360-degree view over the lakes and Alps. A favourite short drive for locals at sunset, and gentle enough for a stroll rather than a hike.

The impossibly pretty lake-and-mountain village whose reflected houses have made it one of Europe's most photographed places, with a 7,000-year salt-mining history above it. Go early or late to have it calm; a private driver makes the scenic Wolfgangsee route part of the pleasure.

A storybook lakeside village around the White Horse Inn of operetta fame, with a rack railway up the Schafberg for a panorama over the whole lake district. A relaxed, elegant stop on the way to or from Hallstatt, with lake terraces made for a long lunch.

A small, dazzlingly clear drinking-water lake ringed by forest, closest of the lakes to the city and home to the Schloss Fuschl estate. An easy first taste of the Salzkammergut — a swim, a lakeside walk, and back for dinner.

The salt that made Salzburg rich, explored underground on miners' wooden slides, a boat across a mirror-still brine lake and a train through the mountain — theatrical fun that lands equally with children and grandparents. Cool year-round; they provide the overalls.

The largest ice cave in the world open to visitors, over 40 kilometres of passages with about a kilometre of glittering frozen cathedrals and waterfalls lit by carbide lamp. A genuine adventure — cold, with steps and a cable car, best for the fitter and more curious of the group.

A 900-year-old cliff-top castle above the Salzach valley, famous for its dramatic falconry demonstrations with eagles and vultures wheeling over the ramparts. It stars in the aerial shots of The Sound of Music, and pairs naturally with the nearby ice cave for a full mountain day.

A working German salt mine turned experience, entered by mine train and slides with a light show across an underground salt lake — a polished alternative to Hallein just over the border. Reliably delightful for children, and cool on a hot summer afternoon.
A monastery beer hall pouring from wooden barrels since 1621 — Austria's largest of its kind, all stone jugs, chestnut garden and unforced local life.
The lakeside castle's handsome main bar — hand-painted alpine murals, classic and inventive cocktails, and an intimate Whisky Room alongside.
Two design-forward bars inside Red Bull's glass hangar — one at ground level, one suspended above the aircraft — with polished, ambitious cocktails.

venues.n: The Sketch Bar & Lounge, Hotel Bristol
venues.d: The grand old Bristol's fireside bar — creative cocktails and long drinks in a calm, old-world room facing the Mirabell Gardens.
